Actions Should EARN Their Credit: Test-Time Adaptation and Route Consolidation for Frozen LLM Agents

Bian Sun Kevin Zhai Mubarak Shah Song Wang ††thanks: Corresponding author: song.wang@ucf.edu Affiliation: University of Central Florida, Institute of Artificial Intelligence
Abstract

LLM agents can use feedback from repeated attempts to improve their decisions without updating model parameters. However, positive action credits can continue to favor actions that repeatedly achieve the same score, even when higher scores are achievable. Under a fixed interaction budget, trying new actions in the final attempts can also lower performance. We introduce EARN, a method that uses past experience to guide further progress and retain earlier performance through conditional reuse of effective action sequences. EARN reduces action credits for reaching scores repeatedly attained in earlier episodes and assigns larger credits to action segments that reach higher scores. These credits adjust the probabilities of LLM-proposed actions. During the final episodes, EARN directly replays stored actions when the current context matches the recorded context and the actions remain available, bypassing LLM candidate generation. We evaluate performance at the end of the interaction budget using the average score over the final four episodes. Across Jericho, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, EARN achieves the best score on this metric in 31 of 33 task–budget settings among the evaluated methods, including ties. Across the evaluated Jericho budgets, replay bypasses 78.9–86.3% of candidate-generation calls in the final four episodes, averaged across games.

   

1 Introduction

Completing interactive tasks, such as text-adventure games, multimodal open-world survival games, and virtual science experiments, typically requires an agent to perform a sequence of actions based on current observations. Because the right action is not always clear, the agent may try different actions, observe their outcomes, and adjust its choices. Specifically, an LLM agent uses the task description, current observations, and interaction records in its prompt to select the next action [1]. If an attempt is unsuccessful, the agent can start again and try a different sequence. Importantly, the earlier attempt still provides useful information [2]. For example, a failed attempt to open a door may reveal that the agent must first obtain a key. Such information is particularly useful in later attempts, when the agent can avoid the same mistake and focus on completing the remaining task. Thus, earlier experience can help the agent make better choices rather than repeat the same failed actions.

Existing methods help agents reuse experience without updating the LLM’s parameters. Specifically, Reflexion stores written reflections to guide later attempts [2], while EvoTest revises prompts, memory, and other agent settings [3]. JitRL more directly adjusts action probabilities using returns from earlier interactions [4]. However, actions that earned points in the past do not necessarily help the agent achieve higher scores. For example, the agent may find a key and open the first door to earn points in every attempt, yet fail to complete the remaining task because it misses an important action. Although these actions remain useful, continuing to prioritize them simply because they previously earned points may lead the agent to repeat the same actions and obtain the same score. Thus, using past results effectively requires distinguishing repeated progress from progress beyond what the agent has already achieved.

Therefore, two challenges arise. (1) Moving beyond previously achieved results. Actions that earned points in earlier attempts may continue to receive positive credit even when they produce no further progress. For example, an agent may repeatedly open the first door but never complete the remaining task. Thus, experience reuse should distinguish previously achieved progress from new gains. (2) Retaining earlier performance. Choosing actions step by step based on past experience does not ensure that an earlier good result will be reproduced. Even after finding an effective action sequence, the agent may choose different actions midway through a later attempt and obtain a lower score. This matters particularly when the number of attempts is limited and only a few remain. Repeating the earlier sequence can reduce this risk, but only when its actions still apply to the current situation. For example, without the key, the agent cannot repeat an action that previously unlocked the door. Therefore, reusing an effective sequence requires checking whether the current conditions still support its execution.

We introduce EARN, a training-free method that uses persistent memory to adjust action probabilities and conditionally reuse a previously effective action sequence (Figure 1). We group consecutive episodes into blocks and select the highest-scoring trajectory from each block. From this trajectory, EARN assigns numerical credits to actions leading up to a score increase, using these credits to guide later choices. Actions receive less credit when the resulting score does not exceed a level reached more than once in earlier episodes. To also use information from the other trajectories, EARN computes step-wise credits after every episode. During action selection, it combines the two credit estimates and reduces the block-wise estimate when few records match the current situation and candidate action, or when their credit values vary substantially. Separately, EARN stores a route containing an ordered action sequence and the situation recorded before each action. During the final episodes, the agent directly executes stored actions while the recorded and current situations match and the actions remain available. Otherwise, it resumes memory-guided action selection.

We evaluate whether this combination of memory-guided decisions and conditional route reuse improves performance in the final episodes across Jericho [5], ScienceWorld [6], and Crafter [7]. Our evaluation covers three aspects: final-four average scores relative to existing baselines, retention of previously achieved scores and inference savings when routes remain executable, and adaptation when task instances change. Together, these experiments assess whether EARN can improve later decisions and reuse accumulated experience under both repeated and changing execution conditions. Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce EARN, a training-free method that combines progress-relative block-wise credit attribution from selected trajectories with step-wise feedback from every episode to adjust candidate-action probabilities through support-controlled fusion without parameter updates.

  • •

    We develop conditional route replay to complement credit-guided action selection. It preserves an applicable route’s action order and reduces LLM candidate-generation calls by directly executing stored actions. When replay stops, memory-guided action selection resumes.

  • •

    We evaluate EARN across three interactive benchmarks. Among the compared methods, EARN achieves the highest or tied-highest final-four average episode score in 14 of 15 Jericho game–budget settings, 14 of 15 ScienceWorld task–budget settings, and all three Crafter budgets.

2 Related Work

Test-time adaptation of LLM agents. Existing methods differ in what they retain from earlier episodes and how the agent uses that information in later decisions. Some methods store text derived from earlier episodes: Reflexion [2] stores verbal reflections on task feedback, CLIN [8] records causal relations between actions and observed effects, and ReasoningBank [9] distills reasoning strategies from successful and failed trajectories. Beyond updating memory, EvoTest [3] revises the agent’s prompt, hyperparameters, and tool-use routines. Other methods store numerical estimates for actions. REMEMBERER [10] retrieves past actions and their estimated scores to guide action selection through the prompt. JitRL [4] is the closest prior method to EARN. It uses an LLM evaluator to assign numerical feedback to actions, computes discounted returns, and averages retrieved returns for each candidate action to adjust action probabilities. EARN instead uses a score repeatedly attained in earlier episodes as a reference for assigning action credits and discounts credits for score increases up to that reference. It combines block-wise credits from one selected trajectory per block with step-wise credits from every episode to adjust action probabilities.

Reusing behavior from earlier episodes. Prior systems represent behavior from earlier interactions as trajectories, textual guidance, workflows, or executable skills. ExpeL [11], Synapse [12], and Self-Generated In-Context Examples [13] use earlier trajectories as in-context examples from which the LLM generates new actions. AutoGuide [14] derives textual guidelines from trajectories and pairs each guideline with a description of the context in which it applies. Agent Workflow Memory [15] derives reusable workflows from trajectories and includes the workflows in prompts for later tasks. Voyager [16] stores executable code skills that can be retrieved and composed. EARN stores a route containing recorded actions and their preceding execution contexts, then directly executes those actions in order while execution checks pass.

3 Problem Formulation

Preliminaries. We consider interactive tasks in which an agent takes a sequence of actions to achieve an objective, and the environment provides observations and scores that indicate task progress. Because a single attempt may leave parts of the task unfinished, attempts allow the agent to try alternative actions and use feedback from earlier attempts. We therefore consider a session of KK episodes of the same task, with a fixed objective and scoring criterion. Each episode kk begins with an environment reset to initial configuration vkv_{k}, which may vary across episodes, and ends upon environment termination or after HH steps, giving a length Tk≤HT_{k}\leq H. At step tt, the agent receives execution context sk,ts_{k,t}, containing the current observation and supplementary information such as available actions, and executes action ak,ta_{k,t}. The environment then returns feedback yk,ty_{k,t}, including the next context, the score change, and a termination indicator. Let Sk,tS_{k,t} denote the running score after action ak,ta_{k,t} and Sk,0S_{k,0} the initial score. The score change at step tt is Sk,t−Sk,t−1S_{k,t}-S_{k,t-1}.

Memory Update and Action Selection. The LLM parameters θ\theta remain fixed throughout the session. Persistent memory ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} retains information from episodes 1,…,k−11,\ldots,k-1, with ℳ1=∅\mathcal{M}_{1}=\varnothing. The agent constructs prompt xk,tx_{k,t} from the task specification, current context, within-episode history, and retrieved memory. An action-selection rule Πθ\Pi_{\theta} uses both the prompt and persistent memory:

ak,t∼Πθ(⋅∣xk,t,ℳk).a_{k,t}\sim\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{k,t},\mathcal{M}_{k}). (1)

The trajectory τk\tau_{k} records the ordered sequence of contexts, actions, and feedback from episode kk:

τk=(sk,t,ak,t,yk,t)t=1Tk.\tau_{k}=\bigl(s_{k,t},a_{k,t},y_{k,t}\bigr)_{t=1}^{T_{k}}. (2)

The task’s scoring criterion assigns episode score SkS_{k} to the completed trajectory. An action credit is instead a numerical value constructed from interaction feedback to guide action selection in later episodes. After each episode, a memory-update rule UU produces the memory for the next episode:

ℳk+1=U⁡(ℳk,τk,Sk).\mathcal{M}_{k+1}=U(\mathcal{M}_{k},\tau_{k},S_{k}). (3)

Goal. We seek a memory-update rule UU and an action-selection rule Πθ\Pi_{\theta} that maximize the expected average score over the final WW episodes, where 1≤W≤K1\leq W\leq K, subject to the episode budget KK and per-episode step limit HH:

Jterm=𝔼agent,environment​[1W​∑k=K−W+1KSk].J_{\mathrm{term}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{agent},\,\mathrm{environment}}\left[\frac{1}{W}\sum_{k=K-W+1}^{K}S_{k}\right]. (4)

4 Method

EARN uses scores repeatedly attained in earlier episodes as a reference for assigning action credits, discounting credits for reaching those scores again. The memory-update rule UU adds step-wise credits after every episode and block-wise credits from score-increase events after selecting one trajectory from each block. The action-selection rule Πθ\Pi_{\theta} retrieves credits to adjust candidate-action probabilities and conditionally replays a stored route. Figure 2 illustrates both credit assignments on one trajectory. Algorithm 1(Appendix C.4) summarizes our methods.

4.1 Learning: Action Credit and Persistent Memory

Block-wise Credit Attribution. To prioritize experience with greater task progress, we compare trajectories within non-overlapping blocks of BB consecutive acquisition episodes and select one per block, primarily by the highest running score reached. This provides several outcomes to compare while allowing later experience to contribute without surpassing the best score of the entire session. To give less credit for progress already achieved, we maintain a progress frontier FbF_{b} using route scores observed multiple times in recent episodes. The frontier starts at zero, never decreases, and is fixed at the start of each block. A score-increase event ee occurs when Sk,te>Sk,te−1S_{k,t_{e}}>S_{k,t_{e}-1}; let Se=Sk,teS_{e}=S_{k,t_{e}}. Because earlier actions may contribute to this increase, we credit a segment rather than only the scoring action. For Se≤FbS_{e}\leq F_{b}, we use a local segment ending at tet_{e}. Otherwise, we use the segment after first reaching or exceeding FbF_{b} through tet_{e}, covering the actions leading to progress beyond the frontier. Appendix C.2 gives the selection, frontier-update, and segment details.

For a segment of LeL_{e} actions, let ce,ic_{e,i} denote the credit assigned to the action at position ii. We assign larger credits to actions closer to the score-increase event and discount credits for repeated progress. The interpolation endpoints ℓe\ell_{e} and heh_{e} depend on the discount coefficient αpre\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}} for repeated progress and the credit offset ρ\rho for progress beyond FbF_{b}:

ce,i=(1−iLe)ℓe+iLehe,(ℓe,he)={(0,αpre),Se≤Fb,(ρ,1),Se>Fb,i=1,…,Le.c_{e,i}=\left(1-\frac{i}{L_{e}}\right)\ell_{e}+\frac{i}{L_{e}}h_{e},\qquad(\ell_{e},h_{e})=\begin{cases}(0,\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}),&S_{e}\leq F_{b},\\ (\rho,1),&S_{e}>F_{b},\end{cases}\quad i=1,\ldots,L_{e}. (5)

Credit increases linearly toward the scoring action. For repeated progress, it receives αpre\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}; for new progress, it receives 1. The offset ρ\rho gives preceding actions positive credit in new-progress segments.

Step-wise Credit Attribution. To provide timely feedback between block-wise updates and retain information from unselected trajectories, we compute step-wise credits after every episode, including replay episodes. For each step tt, we construct a numerical signal r~k,t\tilde{r}_{k,t} from environment feedback and interaction history. A score-increase event contributes 11 if the running score after the event exceeds the progress frontier, and a discounted positive signal otherwise. Here, we use the frontier before updating memory from the current episode. We additionally give small bonuses for previously unobserved outcomes and apply penalties for detected terminal failures. Using temporal discount factor γ\gamma, we accumulate these signals backward through the episode to compute step-wise credit Ck,tstepC^{\mathrm{step}}_{k,t} for action ak,ta_{k,t}:

Ck,tstep=∑u=tTkγu−t​r~k,u.C^{\mathrm{step}}_{k,t}=\sum_{u=t}^{T_{k}}\gamma^{u-t}\tilde{r}_{k,u}. (6)

Here, γ\gamma controls the decay of event feedback as it is propagated backward to preceding actions. An action can receive credit from subsequent events even if it produces no immediate score increase. The resulting credits are stored after each episode, without additional LLM evaluation calls.

Persistent Memory. Persistent memory ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} stores a route ℛk⋆\mathcal{R}_{k}^{\star} and action-credit records ℰk\mathcal{E}_{k}. A route is an ordered action sequence extracted from an episode trajectory, together with the execution context recorded before each action. Each credit record contains an execution context, an action, an assigned credit, and the credit source. Step-wise records are added after every episode; block-wise records from score-increase events are added after selecting a trajectory at block completion. Route storage is independent of block-wise selection: after each episode, the agent considers the new trajectory for route retention based on performance and executability. Details are in Appendix C.

4.2 Adaptation: Adjusting Candidate-Action Probabilities

Given execution context s=sk,ts=s_{k,t}, the agent incorporates retrieved memory into prompt xk,tx_{k,t}. The frozen LLM then proposes candidate actions and reports confidence scores, which we normalize into a base distribution p0​(a∣s)p^{0}(a\mid s) over the candidate set 𝒜⁡(s)\mathcal{A}(s). Additional memory candidates, when enabled, are incorporated as described in Appendix C.5.

Credit Estimates. EARN retrieves block-wise and step-wise credit records from persistent memory ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k}. Semantic retrieval can supplement insufficient exact matches; Appendix C.5 describes this procedure. For block-wise records matching context ss and candidate action aa exactly, let nblkn_{\mathrm{blk}}, μblk\mu_{\mathrm{blk}}, and σblk2\sigma_{\mathrm{blk}}^{2} denote their count, mean, and sample variance. These statistics depend on (s,a)(s,a); we omit the arguments for brevity. To moderate estimates based on limited or inconsistent credit records, we shrink the block-wise estimate toward zero using count-based scaling and a variability correction:

rblk​(s,a)=nblknblk+ν,Qblk​(s,a)=rblk​(s,a)​sgn⁡(μblk)​[|μblk|−ξ​σblk2nblk]+.r_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)=\frac{n_{\mathrm{blk}}}{n_{\mathrm{blk}}+\nu},\qquad Q_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)=r_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)\operatorname{sgn}(\mu_{\mathrm{blk}})\left[|\mu_{\mathrm{blk}}|-\xi\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{blk}}^{2}}{n_{\mathrm{blk}}}}\right]_{+}. (7)

Here, [x]+=max⁡(0,x)[x]_{+}=\max(0,x), ν\nu controls count-based scaling, and ξ\xi controls the variability correction. Without matching records, rblk=Qblk=0r_{\mathrm{blk}}=Q_{\mathrm{blk}}=0. Each retrieved step-wise credit is scaled according to its episode’s replay status and whether the running score before or after the action exceeded that episode’s initial progress frontier. The estimate Qstep​(s,a)Q_{\mathrm{step}}(s,a) is the mean scaled credit over records matching action aa. We center each estimate against its channel’s baseline: Ablk=Qblk−VblkA_{\mathrm{blk}}=Q_{\mathrm{blk}}-V_{\mathrm{blk}} and Astep=Qstep−VstepA_{\mathrm{step}}=Q_{\mathrm{step}}-V_{\mathrm{step}}. These centered estimates express each candidate’s value relative to its channel’s baseline.

Combining Credit Estimates. Because block-wise selection retains only one trajectory per block, step-wise credits use feedback from every episode, including those not selected. When matching block-wise records are sparse, we retain a larger coefficient on the step-wise estimate. As block-wise support grows, we reduce this coefficient to place greater emphasis on credits from selected trajectories. We therefore combine the centered estimates as:

The gates gblk,gstep∈[0,1]g_{\mathrm{blk}},g_{\mathrm{step}}\in[0,1] regulate each channel’s contribution according to retrieved support. The coefficient λstep\lambda_{\mathrm{step}} sets the step-wise scale, η\eta controls its suppression as gblkg_{\mathrm{blk}} increases, and qstepq_{\mathrm{step}} is the largest record-scaling factor among matching step-wise records. The gates and qstepq_{\mathrm{step}} depend on (s,a)(s,a); their arguments are omitted. Step-wise feedback supplements sparse block-wise evidence. We standardize Aℳ​(s,a)A_{\mathcal{M}}(s,a) over the candidate set using its mean and population standard deviation, then clip the result to [−ζ,ζ][-\zeta,\zeta], obtaining A^ℳ​(s,a)\widehat{A}_{\mathcal{M}}(s,a). With adjustment strength β>0\beta>0, the adjusted distribution is

This adjustment shifts the base probability ratio in favor of candidates with higher standardized credit estimates, while retaining the LLM’s base probabilities as a factor. The parameter ζ>0\zeta>0 bounds the standardized estimates. Appendix C.5 describes the numerical handling.

4.3 Conditional Route Replay

Block-wise and step-wise credits adjust candidate-action probabilities, but do not ensure that the agent follows the action order in a stored route ℛk⋆\mathcal{R}_{k}^{\star}. The agent therefore maintains a replayable route separately and conditionally follows its action order when execution checks pass.

Let KcK_{c} denote the number of final episodes scheduled for route replay, with zk=𝕀{k>K−Kc}z_{k}=\mathbb{I}\{k>K-K_{c}\} indicating replay eligibility. The evaluation window WW independently specifies which episode scores enter JtermJ_{\mathrm{term}}. Let mm index the next action am⋆a_{m}^{\star} in ℛk⋆\mathcal{R}_{k}^{\star}. The indicator χk,t∈{0,1}\chi_{k,t}\in\{0,1\} equals one when replay remains active in the episode, a route step remains, the current execution context matches its recorded context, and the action passes availability and terminal-failure checks. The operator Select\operatorname{Select} follows the configured action-selection rule. The agent executes

ak,t={am⋆,zk​χk,t=1,Select(pℳ(⋅∣sk,t)),otherwise.a_{k,t}=\begin{cases}a_{m}^{\star},&z_{k}\chi_{k,t}=1,\\[3.0pt] \operatorname{Select}\!\left(p_{\mathcal{M}}(\cdot\mid s_{k,t})\right),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (10)

Each replayed action advances the route pointer and bypasses LLM candidate generation, while still counting as an environment interaction. A failed execution check or an exhausted route ends replay for the current episode. The agent then resumes candidate generation and uses the block-wise and step-wise credit estimates to adjust action probabilities.

5 Experiments

We organize our experiments around three questions on memory-guided test-time adaptation and final-stage consolidation in LLM agents: Q1: Performance in the final episodes. Does EARN improve performance in the final episodes over the compared baselines across interactive environments? Q2: Performance Retention and Inference Savings. When stored routes are broadly applicable, how reliably does EARN reproduce its best acquired performance, and how many LLM candidate-generation calls does conditional consolidation save? Q3: Experience Transfer. When stored routes are inapplicable, how does EARN use accumulated experience to adapt its decisions and maintain performance in the final episodes?

5.1 Experimental Setup

Environments and Tasks. Experiments span three benchmarks with complementary demand profiles. Jericho  [5] offers parser-based interactive fiction; we adopt the Focus-5 subset (DeepHome, Detective, Zork I, Zork III, ZTUU) and run lifelong sessions of 30×\times30, 50×\times50, and 70×\times70 (episodes ×\times steps per episode). ScienceWorld [6] is evaluated on five tasks, with at most 100 steps per episode and session lengths of 10, 20, and 30 episodes. Task variations alter objects, materials, or environmental configurations across episodes, requiring stored experience to be checked for applicability to the current instance. Crafter [7] is an open-ended survival environment evaluated in a multimodal setting using visual observations and textual context. Performance is measured by the number of distinct achievements unlocked (0–22), with at most 100 steps per episode and session lengths of 10, 20, and 30 episodes.

Compared Approaches. All approaches share an identical frozen W4A16-quantized backbone Gemma-4-31B-Instruct [17], served locally via vLLM [18]. Baselines retain their native decoding, memory, retrieval settings. EARN uses an action-generation temperature of 0.8 across all three benchmarks. EARN uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2 [19] embeddings for semantic retrieval in Jericho and ScienceWorld, exact-context retrieval for action evidence in Crafter. We compare against five baselines that reuse experience while keeping the LLM weights fixed: (1) Reflexion [2], which appends verbal self-critiques of past failures to the prompt; (2) AWM [15], which distills successful episodes into persisted reusable workflows; (3) FIFO Memory, which prepends full episode transcripts under a first-in-first-out context budget; (4) EvoTest [3], which evolves prompts, memory entries, and decoding hyperparameters across episodes; and (5) JitRL [4], which converts returns of past trajectories into advantages that rescale candidate-action probabilities.

Protocol and Metrics. All methods are evaluated under the same episode and step budgets. We report Last-4, SLast​-​4=14​∑k=K−3KSkS_{\mathrm{Last\text{-}4}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{k=K-3}^{K}S_{k}, and Last, SLast=SKS_{\mathrm{Last}}=S_{K}. For Jericho, we additionally report Retention, Rret=14∑k=K−3K𝟏[Sk=S⋆∧S⋆>0]R_{\mathrm{ret}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{k=K-3}^{K}\mathbf{1}[S_{k}=S^{\star}\land S^{\star}>0], where S⋆=max1≤j≤K⁡SjS^{\star}=\max_{1\leq j\leq K}S_{j} is the run’s peak score. Retention measures the fraction of final-window episodes matching a positive peak and is zero for runs without one. EARN enables conditional route replay during the final-four consolidation window. More implementation details are provided in Appendices D.

5.2 Main Results

Performance in the final episodes (Q1). EARN achieves the highest or tied Last-4 score in 14 of 15 Jericho game–budget settings (Table 1) and the best score in 14 of 15 ScienceWorld settings (Table 2), including ties. Crafter results evaluate its performance in multimodal interaction (Table ). Across these settings, the results support the value of selectively reusing accumulated experience for terminal performance, both when stored routes remain applicable and when decisions require adaptation to the current context. Larger interaction budgets do not uniformly yield higher scores, highlighting that how experience is used matters alongside how much is collected. Interaction creates opportunities for progress, but does not by itself ensure that experience will be retained and effectively reused. The comparison highlights the importance of experience selection and context-aware reuse, alongside exploration, for achieving strong performance near the budget endpoint.

Performance Retention and Inference Savings (Q2). When stored routes remain applicable, EARN combines reliable performance reproduction with fewer candidate-generation calls. At 50×5050\times 50 on Jericho, Last-4 retention reaches 1.00 on every game, compared with five-game averages of 0.55 for EvoTest and 0.05 for JitRL (Figure 3). EARN therefore matches its run-best scores throughout the final four episodes, rather than recovering only in the last episode. On Jericho, replay avoids 78.90–86.27% of candidate-generation calls in the final four episodes. These final-window replay steps correspond to whole-run call savings of 4.94–12.39%, averaged equally across games (Figure 4). Retention measures reproduction of each run’s own peak, not global optimality. The saved calls could support additional exploration under a fixed inference budget, although the performance benefit of such reallocation remains untested.

Experience Transfer (Q3). In ScienceWorld, task variations change the environment across episodes, so stored routes may become inapplicable. EARN can still use retrieved experience and action-level evidence to adjust candidate preferences, while generating actions conditioned on the current observation. This separates experience reuse from fixed-route execution: changes in object locations or task requirements need not invalidate all previously acquired evidence. EARN achieves the best or tied Last-4 score in 14 of 15 task–budget settings (Table 2). EARN reuses experience without requiring an entire route to remain applicable: retrieved memory informs candidate generation, while supported action-level evidence adjusts preferences under the current observation. This enables selective reuse of prior experience even when environmental changes prevent direct replay.

5.3 Ablation Study and Method Analysis

Ablation Studies. We remove block-wise credit, step-wise credit, and conditional replay individually on ZTUU and Zork III to assess their contributions to final-episode performance and examine whether the gains come solely from replay. All settings use 30 episodes and 30 steps each. As shown in Table 5, removing either block-wise credit or conditional replay reduces Last-4 from 20.8 to 12.0 on ZTUU and from 4.0 to 3.0 on Zork III. The decline without block-wise credit, even with replay retained, supports contributions from both credit-based action adjustment and route reuse. The effect of step-wise credit varies across tasks: removing it hurts ZTUU, supporting the use of feedback from all trajectories to complement block-wise experience, but improves both Last-4 and Last on Zork III. Additional step-wise feedback therefore does not necessarily improve performance, motivating further analysis of its contribution strength.

Sensitivity Analysis. We vary the suppression coefficient η∈{0,0.5,0.85,1.0}\eta\in\{0,0.5,0.85,1.0\} in Equation 8, keeping λstep=0.35\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}=0.35 and the remaining settings fixed. As shown in Table 5, the default η=0.85\eta=0.85 achieves the highest Last-4 score on ZTUU (20.8). On Zork III, η=1.0\eta=1.0 achieves the highest Last-4 score (4.5), compared with 4.0 for the default; both attain a final-four minimum score of 4.0. On both tasks, η=1.0\eta=1.0 outperforms η=0\eta=0 in Last-4, although performance does not vary monotonically with suppression strength. Thus, retaining a stronger step-wise contribution does not necessarily improve performance. The default performs well on both tested tasks, ranking first on ZTUU and remaining close to the best tested setting on Zork III.

6 Conclusion

We introduced EARN, a training-free method that combines progress-relative block-wise credits with step-wise feedback to adjust candidate-action probabilities. Block-wise selection prioritizes high-performing trajectories, while step-wise updates retain feedback from every episode. Conditional route replay reuses applicable action sequences during the final episodes, bypassing LLM candidate generation and returning to memory-guided selection when replay ends. Across Jericho, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, EARN achieves the best or tied-best Last-4 score in 31 of 33 task–budget settings, with substantial candidate-generation call savings on Jericho. Future work will examine experience reuse under changing conditions and stochastic transitions.

Appendix A Main notation

Appendix B Additional Related Work

Attribution and Credit Assignment in Sequential Decision Making

Credit assignment in sequential decision making aims to determine which historical actions led to delayed outcomes. RUDDER reallocates delayed rewards by decomposing returns, attributing them back to critical decision points; similarly, JitRL estimates the advantage of current candidate actions using returns from past trajectories [20, 4].

Memory Retention

Prior work studies example-level forgetting [21] and memorization dynamics in language models [22]. Continual learning methods mitigate forgetting through parameter regularization [23], episodic-memory constraints [24], and replay with small memory buffers [25]. Experience Replay for Continual Learning [26] uses replay to reduce forgetting, while subsequent work explores interference-based replay selection [27] and preservation of past model outputs [28]. Do Your Best and Get Enough Rest for Continual Learning [29] examines how replay intervals affect retention. Distributionally robust memory evolution dynamically adjusts the memory data distribution to reduce buffer overfitting and alleviate forgetting [30]. In our setting with a frozen model, we define late-stage memory retention as the fraction of final episodes attaining the run’s peak score.

Continual Learning for Agentic Systems

Continual learning requires an agent to retain previously acquired effective behaviors while assimilating new experiences. Voyager achieves long-term capability accumulation in open worlds through automatic curriculum design and an executable skills library, whereas studies like LifelongAgentBench highlight that simply saving and replaying all historical experiences are prone to interference from irrelevant information and context length limitations [16, 31]. Our study addresses cross-episode adaptation under a fixed budget: the environment resets between episodes, but the memory persists.

Appendix C Additional Method Details

C.1 Benchmarks and Tasks

We evaluate on three interactive benchmarks: Jericho, ScienceWorld, and Crafter. The selected environments cover text-based adventure games, scientific tasks, and visual survival gameplay.

Jericho.

Jericho [5] provides text-based interactive fiction environments. Agents read observations and issue commands to navigate locations, inspect objects, and interact with the game world. We use five games:

  • •

    DeepHome. The player explores an abandoned mountain kingdom and prepares it for its inhabitants’ return by restoring essential systems, opening gates, and addressing threats.

  • •

    Detective. The player investigates the mayor’s murder by visiting locations, examining information, collecting objects, and navigating potentially dangerous encounters.

  • •

    Zork I. The player explores the Great Underground Empire, solves puzzles, and collects treasures to return to the trophy case in the white house.

  • •

    Zork III. The player completes trials in the Great Underground Empire to demonstrate worthiness to succeed the Dungeon Master. Progress involves navigation, object use, and interactions with characters.

  • •

    ZTUU. In Zork: The Undiscovered Underground, the player explores a newly discovered underground region and seeks to emerge successfully by navigating rooms and solving object-based puzzles.

ScienceWorld.

ScienceWorld [6] is a text-based simulation environment for elementary science tasks. Agents manipulate objects, use instruments, and perform experiments to satisfy task-specific goals. We evaluate five tasks, each with multiple variations:

  • •

    Conductivity. Test whether a specified material conducts electricity by constructing a circuit and observing its behavior.

  • •

    Unknown Conductivity. Determine the electrical conductivity of an unknown substance through circuit-based testing.

  • •

    Plant. Grow a specified plant by preparing suitable growing conditions and providing the resources needed for its development.

  • •

    Power. Power an electrical component using an energy source that satisfies the requested renewable or nonrenewable category.

  • •

    Melting Known. Measure the melting point of a specified known substance using heating equipment and temperature measurements.

Crafter.

Crafter [7] is a visual, open-world survival game with procedurally generated environments. The agent gathers resources, crafts tools, builds useful structures, and manages survival needs. Progress is measured through 22 achievements, ranging from collecting basic resources to producing advanced tools. These achievements have dependencies, requiring the agent to carry out sequences of preparatory actions. We use a multimodal interface combining visual observations with textual information.

Memory storage.

Alongside the stored route and action-credit records, persistent memory retains aggregate credit statistics and trajectories awaiting block-wise selection.

C.2 Block Size and Progress Frontier

Block size.

We use blocks of B=5B=5 acquisition episodes and select the best-performing trajectory within each block for milestone credit attribution. This provides several trajectories for comparison while keeping the delay before block-wise memory updates short. Smaller blocks offer fewer alternatives, whereas larger blocks delay the use of selected experience. Step-wise credit records continue to update after every episode.

This choice is inspired by self-consistency: Wang et al. [32] suggest starting with five or ten reasoning paths to balance performance and computational cost. Unlike their answer aggregation procedure, EARN selects among sequential interaction trajectories using environment feedback. We therefore adopt B=5B=5 as a practical setting.

Progress Frontier.

Let PkP_{k} denote the route score from episode kk used to update the progress frontier. We locate the first action that reaches the episode’s highest total score. If this action terminates the environment, PkP_{k} is the score immediately before it; otherwise, PkP_{k} is the score immediately after it. This rule also applies to successful termination.

After episode kk, we consider the most recent WF=5W_{F}=5 episodes, including episode kk, indexed by 𝒲k={max⁡(1,k−WF+1),…,k}\mathcal{W}_{k}=\{\max(1,k-W_{F}+1),\ldots,k\}. We round each PjP_{j} to six decimal places before comparing values. The candidate frontier is the highest positive route score recorded in at least two episodes within this window:

F^k=max({0}∪{r>0:∑j∈𝒲k𝟏[Pj=r]≥2}).\widehat{F}_{k}=\max\left(\{0\}\cup\left\{r>0:\sum_{j\in\mathcal{W}_{k}}\mathbf{1}[P_{j}=r]\geq 2\right\}\right). (11)

Here, 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function. Each episode contributes one route score, rather than all intermediate scores along its trajectory.

Let FksysF^{\mathrm{sys}}_{k} denote the progress frontier after episode kk. We initialize it to zero and update it without allowing decreases:

F0sys=0,Fksys=max⁡(Fk−1sys,F^k).F^{\mathrm{sys}}_{0}=0,\qquad F^{\mathrm{sys}}_{k}=\max\left(F^{\mathrm{sys}}_{k-1},\widehat{F}_{k}\right). (12)

If no positive route score appears at least twice in the window, F^k=0\widehat{F}_{k}=0 and the frontier remains unchanged.

Let kbk_{b} denote the first episode of block bb. We fix the block’s frontier before that episode:

Fb=Fkb−1sys.F_{b}=F^{\mathrm{sys}}_{k_{b}-1}. (13)

All block-wise credit attribution in block bb uses this fixed value, even if the system frontier changes during the block. When Fb=0F_{b}=0, the new-progress segment starts at the beginning of the trajectory, subject to the segment-length limit.

Example of Frontier Updates.

Suppose a block has just ended, the frontier before the latest update is 10, and the five most recent route scores are (10,12,10,15,12)(10,12,10,15,12). The candidate frontier is F^k=12\widehat{F}_{k}=12: both 10 and 12 appear twice, whereas 15 appears only once. Thus, Fksys=max⁡(10,12)=12F^{\mathrm{sys}}_{k}=\max(10,12)=12. If the next episode starts a new block, that block uses Fb=12F_{b}=12. Score-increase events ending at or below 12 receive reduced credit, while those ending above 12 receive higher credit. The block’s reference remains fixed at 12 throughout the block.

Trajectory selection and credited segments.

After comparing the highest total scores, trajectory selection breaks ties by the score of the replayable prefix, fewer steps to the highest score, absence of terminal failure at that point, fewer local cycles, and earlier episode, in that order. Let tet_{e} be the step of the eeth score increase in the selected trajectory, so Se=Sk,teS_{e}=S_{k,t_{e}}. If Se≤FbS_{e}\leq F_{b}, the credited segment begins after the preceding score increase. If Se>FbS_{e}>F_{b}, the segment begins after the trajectory first reaches or exceeds FbF_{b}; when the score increase at tet_{e} first crosses FbF_{b}, the segment instead begins after the preceding score increase. Each segment ends at tet_{e} and retains only the most recent actions if its length exceeds the configured limit. We use ρ=1/2\rho=1/2 in Equation 5. We limit repeated admission of identical action segments.

Notation for Block-wise Credit Attribution.

The symbols in the credit attribution formula are defined as follows:

  • •

    ee: A scoring event in the selected trajectory, corresponding to a positive increase in the environment score. A trajectory may contain multiple scoring events.

  • •

    LeL_{e}: The number of actions in the attribution segment associated with event ee.

  • •

    ii: The action’s position within this segment, indexed from 11 to LeL_{e}. The final position i=Lei=L_{e} corresponds to the scoring action.

  • •

    ℓe\ell_{e}: The initial reference value for interpolation, corresponding to relative position i/Le=0i/L_{e}=0. It equals 00 for repeated progress and ρ\rho for new progress.

  • •

    heh_{e}: The terminal interpolation value, equal to the scoring action’s credit. It equals αpre\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}} for repeated progress and 11 for new progress.

  • •

    ce,ic_{e,i}: The credit assigned to the ii-th action in the segment for event ee.

Since ii starts at 11, the first action receives ℓe+(he−ℓe)/Le\ell_{e}+(h_{e}-\ell_{e})/L_{e}, rather than ℓe\ell_{e}. The final action receives heh_{e}.

C.3 Block-wise Credit Estimates

For execution context ss and candidate action aa, let {cj}j=1nblk\{c_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n_{\mathrm{blk}}} denote the block-wise credits in records matching both ss and aa exactly. For nblk>0n_{\mathrm{blk}}>0, their mean μblk\mu_{\mathrm{blk}} and sample variance σblk2\sigma_{\mathrm{blk}}^{2} are:

μblk=1nblk​∑j=1nblkcj,σblk2={1nblk−1​∑j=1nblk(cj−μblk)2,nblk>1,0,nblk=1.\mu_{\mathrm{blk}}=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{blk}}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\mathrm{blk}}}c_{j},\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{blk}}^{2}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{blk}}-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\mathrm{blk}}}(c_{j}-\mu_{\mathrm{blk}})^{2},&n_{\mathrm{blk}}>1,\\[6.0pt] 0,&n_{\mathrm{blk}}=1.\end{cases} (14)

The number of matching records nblkn_{\mathrm{blk}} is not an independent sample size: credits may come from the same trajectory.

For nblk>0n_{\mathrm{blk}}>0, the scaling factor is rblk​(s,a)=nblk/(nblk+ν)r_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)=n_{\mathrm{blk}}/(n_{\mathrm{blk}}+\nu); we set rblk​(s,a)=0r_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)=0 when no records match. When ν=0\nu=0 and at least one record matches, rblk​(s,a)=1r_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)=1. The centering mean Vblk​(s)V_{\mathrm{blk}}(s) averages the block-wise credit estimates Qblk​(s,a)Q_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a) over candidate actions 𝒜⁡(s)\mathcal{A}(s):

Vblk​(s)={∑a∈𝒜⁡(s)rblk​(s,a)​Qblk​(s,a)∑a∈𝒜⁡(s)rblk​(s,a),∑a∈𝒜⁡(s)rblk​(s,a)>0,0,otherwise.V_{\mathrm{blk}}(s)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}(s)}r_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)Q_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)}{\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}(s)}r_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)},&\displaystyle\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}(s)}r_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)>0,\\[10.0pt] 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (15)

For nblk=0n_{\mathrm{blk}}=0, we set Qblk​(s,a)=0Q_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)=0 without evaluating Equation 7. For nblk=1n_{\mathrm{blk}}=1, we set the sample variance to zero, so only the scaling factor rblkr_{\mathrm{blk}} reduces the estimate. A single credit does not establish that later executions will receive the same credit. The variance correction in Equation 7 reduces the magnitude of the block-wise credit estimate toward zero without reversing its sign. We fix ν=3\nu=3, so three matching records receive a count-based scaling factor of 0.50.5. A single record can still contribute, but receives less weight, which increases as more records accumulate. We fix ξ=0.5\xi=0.5 to account for variation among credit records. For the same mean, variance, and record count, this is more conservative than no variability correction (ξ=0\xi=0), while retaining at least as much credit magnitude as a unit correction (ξ=1\xi=1).

C.4 Step-wise Credit Estimates

Let 𝒩⁡(s)\mathcal{N}(s) denote the step-wise credit records retrieved for execution context ss, including records from similar observations when semantic retrieval is enabled. Let 𝒩⁡(s,a)\mathcal{N}(s,a) denote the subset whose actions match candidate action aa. For record jj, let CjstepC_{j}^{\mathrm{step}} be its assigned step-wise credit. We multiply each credit by a scaling factor qjq_{j}:

qj={qreplay,episode designated for route replay,1,other episode, with progress beyond its initial frontier,qpre,otherwise.q_{j}=\begin{cases}q_{\mathrm{replay}},&\text{episode designated for route replay},\\ 1,&\text{other episode, with progress beyond its initial frontier},\\ q_{\mathrm{pre}},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (16)

Progress beyond the episode’s initial frontier means that the total score immediately before or after the action exceeds the progress frontier before that episode’s memory update. The configured factors qreplayq_{\mathrm{replay}} and qpreq_{\mathrm{pre}} scale credits from replay episodes and other credits at or below the frontier, respectively. Credits from replay episodes receive qreplayq_{\mathrm{replay}} regardless of total score. For nonempty 𝒩⁡(s)\mathcal{N}(s), the centering mean Vstep​(s)V_{\mathrm{step}}(s) is

Vstep​(s)=∑j∈𝒩⁡(s)qj​Cjstep|𝒩⁡(s)|.V_{\mathrm{step}}(s)=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(s)}q_{j}C_{j}^{\mathrm{step}}}{|\mathcal{N}(s)|}. (17)

The step-wise credit estimate Qstep​(s,a)Q_{\mathrm{step}}(s,a) averages qj​Cjstepq_{j}C_{j}^{\mathrm{step}} over 𝒩⁡(s,a)\mathcal{N}(s,a), whereas Vstep​(s)V_{\mathrm{step}}(s) averages over all retrieved step-wise records 𝒩⁡(s)\mathcal{N}(s). Both denominators count records; neither denominator sums the scaling factors.

If no step-wise records match candidate action aa, the step-wise gate gstepg_{\mathrm{step}} is zero and that action receives no step-wise contribution to the combined credit estimate Aℳ​(s,a)A_{\mathcal{M}}(s,a).

Support Gates.

Support gates allow limited evidence to influence decisions while reducing its contribution when few records match. For ordinary exact-context block-wise retrieval, we use

gblk​(s,a)={0,nblk=0,nblknblk+κ,0<nblk<mblk,1,nblk≥mblk,g_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)=\begin{cases}0,&n_{\mathrm{blk}}=0,\\ \dfrac{n_{\mathrm{blk}}}{n_{\mathrm{blk}}+\kappa},&0<n_{\mathrm{blk}}<m_{\mathrm{blk}},\\ 1,&n_{\mathrm{blk}}\geq m_{\mathrm{blk}},\end{cases} (18)

with mblk=2m_{\mathrm{blk}}=2 and κ=0.8\kappa=0.8. Thus, a single matching record receives a gate of approximately 0.560.56, while two or more records receive a gate of 11. This allows an initial observation to contribute without giving it the full channel weight.

For step-wise retrieval, let nstep=|𝒩⁡(s,a)|n_{\mathrm{step}}=|\mathcal{N}(s,a)| be the number of matching records. We use

gstep​(s,a)=min⁡(1,nstepmstep)g_{\mathrm{step}}(s,a)=\min\left(1,\frac{n_{\mathrm{step}}}{m_{\mathrm{step}}}\right) (19)

This gate increases linearly with the record count and reaches 11 at three records. We set mstep=3m_{\mathrm{step}}=3, giving gate values of 1/31/3, 2/32/3, and 11 for one, two, and three matching records, respectively. This gradually increases the step-wise contribution as records accumulate. Both gates operate before standardization.

C.5 Action Selection and Route Replay

Context and Action Matching.

Execution contexts combine normalized observations with supplementary state information and an environment-provided state identifier when available. Actions are matched after normalizing case, whitespace, and surrounding punctuation.

Retrieval from Similar Observations.

In Jericho and ScienceWorld, semantic retrieval supplements insufficient exact matches with records from similar observations. For block-wise retrieval, estimates from similar contexts are combined using observation-similarity weights and a transfer coefficient. Step-wise retrieval instead pools additional records before estimating action values. For Crafter, we disable this observation-text retrieval mechanism in our multimodal configuration and use exact-context retrieval for action evidence. Similarity-based retrieval does not replace the context checks required for route replay.

Memory-Based Probability Adjustment.

We normalize the LLM-reported confidence scores. When memory candidates are added, we assign them initial weights and renormalize to obtain p0​(a∣s)p^{0}(a\mid s). Fused advantages are standardized using the candidate mean and population standard deviation, then clipped to [−ζ,ζ][-\zeta,\zeta]. If the standard deviation is below 10−810^{-8}, the divisor is replaced by the larger of one and the maximum absolute centered advantage. Base probabilities are floored at 10−1210^{-12} before taking logarithms. We fix ζ=3\zeta=3 and clip standardized estimates to [−3,3][-3,3] before probability adjustment, bounding the credit-dependent exponent to [−3​β,3​β][-3\beta,3\beta]. For a final candidate set of at most five actions, population-standardized estimates lie within [−2,2][-2,2], so this bound leaves them unchanged.

Route Storage and Replay.

Route memory is updated after each episode, independently of block-wise credit attribution. Candidate routes are compared by score, with shorter routes preferred when scores tie. Before each replayed action, the agent checks context agreement, action availability when a valid-action list is supplied, and stored failure-based restrictions. A failed check or exhausted route ends replay for the current episode, and the agent resumes memory-guided candidate generation and probability adjustment.

Appendix D Additional Experimental Settings

Evaluation window and replay schedule.

We evaluate the final W=4W=4 episodes and use blocks of B=5B=5 episodes for block-wise credit attribution. The evaluation window and block size are separate protocol choices. Conditional route replay is enabled in the final four episodes. Step-wise credit attribution uses every episode, including episodes designated for replay.

Hyperparameters and Hardware.

  • •

    Discount factor (γ=0.95\gamma=0.95). This setting allows scoring-event feedback to reach earlier preparatory actions while decaying with temporal distance. An action occurring ten steps before a scoring event receives that event’s signal with a discount weight of 0.9510≈0.600.95^{10}\approx 0.60.

  • •

    Probability-adjustment strength (β=0.75\beta=0.75). This coefficient controls how strongly memory changes the base action probabilities. When two candidates differ by one unit in their standardized and clipped credit estimates, the adjustment multiplies their base probability ratio by e0.75≈2.12e^{0.75}\approx 2.12 in favor of the higher-valued candidate. Memory can therefore meaningfully influence selection while the LLM’s base distribution continues to contribute to the adjusted probabilities.

  • •

    Block-wise credit parameters (αpre=0.02\alpha_{\mathrm{pre}}=0.02, ρ=0.5\rho=0.5). For repeated-progress segments, credits follow 0.02​i/Le0.02i/L_{e}, reaching 0.02 at the scoring action. For new-progress segments, credits follow 0.5+0.5​i/Le0.5+0.5i/L_{e}, reaching 1 at the scoring action. This assigns higher credit to new progress while retaining small positive credits for repeated progress.

  • •

    Base step-wise weight (λstep=0.35\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}=0.35). The base weight of step-wise credit is fixed at 0.35. Its contribution to the combined estimate is further regulated by block-wise support, the step-wise support gate, and record scaling.

  • •

    Step-wise suppression coefficient (η=0.85\eta=0.85). The block-wise support gate gblk​(s,a)∈[0,1]g_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)\in[0,1] modulates the step-wise coefficient:

    λstep​[1−η​gblk​(s,a)]+=0.35​[1−0.85​gblk​(s,a)]+.\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}[1-\eta g_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)]_{+}=0.35[1-0.85g_{\mathrm{blk}}(s,a)]_{+}.

    This coefficient decreases from 0.35 when gblk=0g_{\mathrm{blk}}=0 to 0.0525 when gblk=1g_{\mathrm{blk}}=1, before applying the step-wise gate gstepg_{\mathrm{step}} and record scale qstepq_{\mathrm{step}}. Thus, stronger block-wise support attenuates the step-wise contribution before standardization without eliminating it through suppression alone.

For EARN, the generation temperature is 0.8, and the LLM is requested to propose five candidate actions per decision. We serve the W4A16-quantized Gemma-4-31B-it checkpoint using vLLM on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. Model parameters remain frozen throughout evaluation.

Appendix E Inference Savings from Conditional Replay

Measurement.

We measure how conditional replay reduces LLM candidate-generation calls on the Jericho runs reported in Table 1. A replayed action is still executed in the environment, but bypasses LLM candidate generation. Thus, each replayed step avoids one logical generation call without reducing the number of environment interactions. We count replayed steps from transition logs and verify that non-replay steps match the corresponding decision-history records. This measurement excludes API retries, token consumption, and latency.

Metrics.

For game gg, let Tg,kT_{g,k} denote the number of executed steps in episode kk, and let Ng,kreplayN^{\mathrm{replay}}_{g,k} denote the number of directly replayed steps. Table 7 reports three percentages:

SavegLast​-​4\displaystyle\mathrm{Save}_{g}^{\mathrm{Last\text{-}4}} =1004​∑k=K−3KNg,kreplayTg,k,\displaystyle=\frac{100}{4}\sum_{k=K-3}^{K}\frac{N^{\mathrm{replay}}_{g,k}}{T_{g,k}}, (20)
SavegLast\displaystyle\mathrm{Save}_{g}^{\mathrm{Last}} =100​Ng,KreplayTg,K,\displaystyle=100\frac{N^{\mathrm{replay}}_{g,K}}{T_{g,K}},
SavegFinal/Run\displaystyle\mathrm{Save}_{g}^{\mathrm{Final/Run}} =100​∑k=K−3KNg,kreplay∑k=1KTg,k.\displaystyle=100\frac{\sum_{k=K-3}^{K}N^{\mathrm{replay}}_{g,k}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}T_{g,k}}.

Last-4 averages the per-episode saving rates over the final four episodes, and Last reports the final episode’s rate. Final/Run divides replayed steps in the final four episodes by all executed steps in the run. Each reported average gives equal weight to the five games.

Results.

Conditional replay avoids 78.90–86.27% of candidate-generation calls in the final four episodes, averaged equally across games. These final-window savings correspond to 12.39%, 7.76%, and 4.94% of all executed steps under the 30/30, 50/50, and 70/70 budgets, respectively. When replay becomes inapplicable, the agent resumes LLM candidate generation and probability adjustment. These counts measure the generation calls bypassed during the recorded runs. They do not measure how episode scores would change if the agent generated an action at every step.

Appendix F Case Study

Case analysis.

Figure 5 shows that the key to conditional replay is that it reuses a validated route prefix without locking the agent into the entire stored trajectory. Block-wise credit emphasizes progress in high-performing trajectories, while step-wise credit retains feedback from other episodes; when replay no longer applies, the agent can return to memory-guided action generation. ZTUU’s final episode illustrates this flexibility. The first 22 replayed steps bring the score to 12. After the replay diverges at step 22, the agent resumes generation, obtains further progress through take red lens and take coin, and recovers its previous best score of 22.

Thus, replay preserves a reliable prefix while leaving the remaining steps open to adaptation, rather than forcing the agent to repeat an entire old route. The avoided LLM calls could potentially be reallocated to additional exploration under a fixed call budget, provided further environment interactions are available; this reallocation is not evaluated here.

Appendix G Additional Controlled Comparisons

G.1 Baselines with Their Native Implementations

We run Reflexion, AWM, EvoTest, and JitRL following the protocols in their publicly available implementations. Each retains its method-specific decoding, memory, and retrieval settings. For FIFO Memory, we prepend full transcripts of previous episodes to the prompt and remove the oldest transcripts when the memory context budget is exceeded. Within each benchmark, all methods use the same frozen backbone, task instances, interaction budgets, and scoring protocol. This preserves their distinct decision mechanisms while controlling the model and evaluation conditions.

G.2 EARN under the Matched Evaluation Protocol

EARN uses the same backbone and evaluation protocol as the baselines, without parameter updates. For EARN, we set the action-generation temperature to 0.8 across all three benchmarks, five candidate actions, and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings for semantic retrieval.
